sources.news_title: "You'd think we would've learned that lesson by now": Obama says US can't "bomb" way to Iran deal
sources.text:
Barack Obama is deeply skeptical that the United States and Iran will be able to work out a deal better than the one that was in place before President Donald Trump‘s first term.
The Obama administration reached a deal with Iran in 2015. That deal saw Iran agreeing to limit its nuclear program, in exchange for an easing of sanctions put in place by the United States and the UN. President Donald Trump withdrew from the deal in 2018.
Obama discussed the withdrawal and subsequent war with Iran in an interview with ABC‘s Robin Roberts on Sunday.
“It is doubtful that any agreement that arises is going to be significantly different or a significant improvement from the deal that we had in the first place,” he said.
The former president, who led a large troop surge in Afghanistan and massively expanded the U.S. drone warfare program, said that the US can’t “bomb [its] way” to foreign policy solutions. Though he admitted that a show of force may “sometimes seem appealing,” he said there’s no substitute for taking the time to talk out a deal.
“You’d think we would’ve learned that lesson by now, but it seems like every so often we have to learn that lesson again,” he said.

Trump has been deeply critical of the former agreement between Iran and the US. In his first term, he called it a “horrible one-sided deal that should have never, ever been made.”
“It didn’t bring calm, it didn’t bring peace, and it never will,” he said.
Trump has promised to work out a better deal in a ceasefire agreement with Iran. That ceasefire has been promised as days away for weeks, though no deal has been made public.

sources.news_title: Obama says it's 'doubtful' Trump's Iran deal will differ from 2015 framework
sources.text:
Former President Barack Obama said it is “doubtful” that President Donald Trump’s emerging agreement with Iran will differ significantly from the 2015 nuclear deal negotiated during his administration.
Speaking to ABC News’s Robin Roberts in an interview preview released Sunday, Obama said any agreement reached by the Trump administration would likely resemble the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action, the multinational accord Trump withdrew from during his first term.
Recommended Stories
“It is doubtful that any agreement that arises is going to be significantly different or a significant improvement from the deal that we had in the first place and had worked for for a long stretch of time before we, the United States, pulled out of it,” Obama said.
The comments come as Trump says the U.S. is in the final stretch of finalizing an agreement with Tehran following months of military conflict and negotiations. The president has repeatedly suggested a deal could be reached quickly and argued that any accord produced by his administration would be stronger than the Obama-era framework.
“Unlike Obama’s Hundreds of Billions of Dollars in payments to them, including 1.7 Billion Dollars in green, cold cash, no money will exchange hands,” Trump wrote on Saturday.
The 2015 nuclear agreement, negotiated by the United States, Iran, and five other world powers, imposed restrictions on Iran’s nuclear program in exchange for sanctions relief. Trump withdrew the U.S. from the accord in 2018, calling it one of the worst agreements ever negotiated and reimposing sanctions on Tehran through a “maximum pressure” campaign.
Obama defended diplomacy as a tool for addressing Iran’s nuclear ambitions, saying the latest negotiations demonstrate the limits of military force alone.
“In retrospect, it’s a reminder that on a lot of difficult foreign policy problems, the notion that we can just bully our way or bomb our way to solutions may sometimes seem appealing,” Obama said. “The fact of the matter is taking the time to explore diplomacy and exhaust the possibilities of coming up with deals that don’t solve 100% of the problem, but solve 80%, 90% of the problem, while avoiding the necessity of going to war, you’d think we would have learned that lesson by now.”
The Trump administration has rejected the comparison between the emerging agreement and the JCPOA.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth argued Sunday that the key distinction is the leverage Trump created through military action against Iran.
“We bombed Iran and then put in a blockade and then ran ships through and then have restarted when necessary to ensure that they come to the table for a great deal,” Hegseth said. “That’s the big difference between this and JCPOA and the way Obama did it.”
Hegseth said the administration negotiated “from a position of strength” and pledged to maintain military pressure on Tehran as talks continue.
“President Trump led with military might,” Hegseth said. “That military might will stay as long as necessary.”
Under the proposed deal, which is under review by Tehran, Iran would agree to end all nuclear ambitions and would meet with Washington to find a path to removing all remaining uranium from the country.

sources.news_title: Obama says Trump Iran deal will not improve on his pact
sources.text:
Barack Obama said it was unrealistic to expect that any deal between U.S. President Donald Trump and Tehran would mark a "significant improvement" over his own nuclear pact 11 years ago.
In interview excerpts released Sunday on ABC News talk show "This Week," the former President also suggested it was better to negotiate a deal that falls short of all of Washington's requirements in order to avoid an outright war.
"It is doubtful that any agreement that arises is going to be significantly different or a significant improvement from the deal that we had in the first place," Mr. Obama said, referring to 2015's landmark pact that Mr. Trump abandoned.
Mr. Obama said his own deal "had worked for a long stretch of time before... the United States pulled out of it."
US and Israeli forces sparked the Middle East war in late February when they launched strikes against Iran. For months Trump has bandied about a potential peace deal with the Islamic republic, but that country's leaders have yet to sign on.
Mr. Trump has stressed the deal, which he says would forever block Iran's ability to produce a nuclear weapon and would lead to the immediate opening of the blockaded Strait of Hormuz, could be signed on Sunday.
Tehran has not confirmed it will yet sign a deal, saying that for now there was "no point" in peace talks with the United States.
Mr. Obama said the troubled progress of a new U.S.-Iran deal is a reminder that Washington can not "just bully our way or bomb our way to solutions" instead of engaging in comprehensive diplomacy.
"You'd think we would have learned that lesson by now," he said.

sources.news_title: Obama ‘doubtful’ Trump’s Iran deal will be different than the one he signed in 2015
Obama says Trump's Iran deal may end up looking like one he abandoned, warns against 'bombing our way' to solutions
sources.text:
Former US President Barack Obama has weighed in on the ongoing efforts to secure a new agreement between Washington and Tehran, arguing that any eventual deal is unlikely to be dramatically different from the landmark nuclear accord his administration negotiated more than a decade ago.
Speaking to ABC News in an interview scheduled to air in full on Wednesday, Obama questioned whether the current diplomatic push would produce anything substantially better than the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), the 2015 nuclear agreement that President Donald Trump withdrew from during his first term in office.
His remarks come at a time when the United States and Iran appear to be inching toward a framework agreement that could reopen the Strait of Hormuz, ease sanctions on Tehran and establish a roadmap for future negotiations on Iran's nuclear programme.
Obama: New deal unlikely to be very different
Reflecting on the ongoing negotiations, Obama suggested that the broad contours of any future agreement would likely resemble the framework already reached under the JCPOA.
"It is doubtful that any agreement that arises is going to be significantly different, or a significant improvement, from the deal that we had in the first place and had worked for, for a long stretch of time, before we, the United States pulled out of it," Obama told ABC News.
The former president's comments amount to a direct defence of the agreement negotiated by his administration and a subtle criticism of Washington's decision to abandon it.
What was the JCPOA?
The Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action was signed in 2015 between Iran and six world powers, including the United States.
Under the agreement, Iran accepted strict limits on its nuclear programme, including restrictions on uranium enrichment and enhanced inspections by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA).
In return, Tehran received relief from international sanctions, regained access to frozen assets and was allowed to resume significant oil exports.
Supporters argued the deal effectively blocked Iran's pathway to a nuclear weapon while avoiding another military conflict in the Middle East.
Critics, including Trump and many Republicans, argued that the agreement provided Iran with economic benefits while only temporarily restricting its nuclear activities.
Trump formally withdrew the United States from the accord in 2018 and reimposed sweeping sanctions on Tehran.
Current talks echo the original deal
The negotiations currently underway appear to contain several elements that closely resemble the structure of the original JCPOA.
According to details of a draft memorandum discussed by US and Iranian officials, the framework under consideration reportedly includes limits on Iran's nuclear activities, discussions over uranium enrichment, sanctions relief and the release of billions of dollars in frozen Iranian assets.
Reports have also suggested that the proposed agreement could involve the eventual lifting of US and UN sanctions, temporary waivers for Iranian oil exports and negotiations over Tehran's stockpile of highly enriched uranium.
The draft framework also seeks to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, a vital energy corridor through which roughly one-fifth of global oil supplies pass.
These provisions have led many analysts to note similarities with the original nuclear deal, albeit in a vastly different geopolitical environment shaped by months of conflict between Iran, Israel and the United States.
Diplomacy over military action
Obama also used the interview to argue that diplomacy remains the most effective way to address the Iranian challenge.
He expressed hope that the ongoing violence in the region would come to an end.
"I hope that bombing stops and ordinary people are no longer suffering as a consequence of the war," he said.
The former president warned against relying exclusively on military force to solve complex geopolitical disputes.
He criticised "the notion that we can just bully our way or bomb our way into solutions."
Instead, Obama called for sustained negotiations even if they fail to resolve every issue.
"Taking the time to explore diplomacy and exhaust the possibilities of coming up with deals that don't solve 100% of the problem but solve 80, 90% of the problem while avoiding the necessity of going to war."
He added: "You'd think we would have learned that lesson by now, but it seems like every so often we have to relearn that lesson again."
Deal still faces obstacles
Obama's remarks come as negotiators continue to wrestle with several unresolved issues.
Iran has insisted on preserving its right to enrich uranium and maintaining a role in managing traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. The United States has pushed for tighter restrictions on Tehran's nuclear activities and broader regional security guarantees.
Israeli officials have also expressed concerns about any agreement that would allow Iran to retain elements of its nuclear infrastructure.
Despite growing optimism from Washington and some regional mediators, Tehran has repeatedly stated that no final decision has yet been taken.
Still, as diplomats work toward a possible breakthrough, Obama's intervention has revived a central question hanging over the negotiations: after years of conflict, sanctions and military confrontation, could the United States ultimately end up returning to a framework remarkably similar to the one it walked away from in 2018?
